did_you_know.text: Did you know? Ecclesiastes sets a good name alongside good oil and gives priority to the good name; he also presents the day of death as a more meaningful point for reflection than the day of birth.

Did you know? According to Ecclesiastes, a house of mourning may teach a person more than a house of feasting, because it reminds them of every person’s end and encourages the living to reflect on their ways.
Did you know? Ecclesiastes prefers the rebuke of a wise person to the songs of fools, because criticism can correct a person, while empty amusement may remain shallow and fleeting.
Did you know? The laughter of fools is compared to the sound of burning thorns beneath a pot: noisy and brief, yet lacking lasting usefulness. That is why it is also called “vanity” in the verse.
Did you know? Ecclesiastes warns that oppression does not harm only the weak; it can also affect the wise and undermine their judgment. The verse adds that a gift or bribe can corrupt the heart.
Did you know? Ecclesiastes emphasizes that the outcome or end may prove better than the beginning, and he places patience above pride.

Did you know? Ecclesiastes opposes idealizing the past: the question “Why were the former days better than these?” is not necessarily presented as a question of wisdom, because the past is not always as we remember it.
Did you know? Ecclesiastes describes both wisdom and money as a protective shade, but gives wisdom a unique advantage: it can preserve the life of its possessor.

Did you know? Ecclesiastes notes that reality does not always present immediate and clear rewards: he saw a righteous person perish despite their righteousness and a wicked person live long in their wickedness.

Did you know? The chapter concludes that God made human beings upright, but they sought out “many schemes” for themselves—plots, plans, and complicated ways that departed from their original uprightness.
